payload.original: Historical investigation from official and archival sources. Scope: the June 1972 DNC break-in, initial investigations and public explanations, congressional testimony and discovery of the White House recording system, access to recordings, evidence of concealment and obstruction, and institutional and constitutional consequences. Source posture and date are preserved so testimony and contemporary claims are not silently upgraded to later findings.
payload.title: Watergate: The Break-In and Cover-Up, 1972-1974

payload.original: On 17 June 1972, five men were arrested inside Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate complex while attempting to repair surveillance equipment installed during an earlier entry. [W-C001]
On 30 August 1972, President Nixon announced that John Dean had investigated the matter and found no involvement by White House personnel. [W-C003]
Seven men were indicted on 15 September 1972 for their roles in the June break-in; five pleaded guilty and two were convicted in January 1973. [W-C004]
The Senate created the Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities on 7 February 1973 to investigate the 1972 election campaign and related conduct. [W-C005]
In public Senate testimony, former White House counsel John Dean alleged that President Nixon approved plans to conceal White House involvement in the break-in. [W-C006]
On 16 July 1973, Alexander Butterfield testified that President Nixon had installed a voice-activated system that automatically recorded Oval Office conversations. [W-C007]
On 23 July 1973, the Senate committee and Special Prosecutor Cox subpoenaed White House tapes and documents; President Nixon refused to comply with Cox's subpoena on 25 July. [W-C008]

On 20 October 1973, Attorney General Elliot Richardson refused the President's order to dismiss special prosecutor Archibald Cox and resigned; Acting Attorney General Robert Bork then dismissed Cox. [W-C009]
The White House disclosed that one subpoenaed conversation contained an approximately 18.5-minute gap; the available official chronology does not establish who caused the erasure or why. [W-C010]
White House Tape 741-2 records a 23 June 1972 Oval Office conversation between President Nixon and H. R. Haldeman, six days after the arrests. [W-C011]

The Nixon Library's description of Conversation 741-2 says Nixon and Haldeman discussed the FBI's tracing of Watergate money and a proposal that CIA officials ask the FBI to halt that line of investigation on national-security grounds. [W-C012]

On 1 March 1974, a federal grand jury indicted seven former presidential aides and named the President as an unindicted co-conspirator in sealed materials considered in United States v. Nixon. [W-C013]
The Watergate Road Map was a grand-jury report consisting of a two-page summary, 53 numbered statements, and 97 supporting documents transmitted under seal to the House Judiciary Committee. [W-C014]

The Supreme Court unanimously held that a generalized interest in confidentiality did not justify an absolute presidential privilege against a demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a pending criminal trial. [W-C016]

The House Judiciary Committee's first proposed article of impeachment found that the President and his agents pursued a course of conduct designed to delay, impede, and obstruct investigation of the Watergate entry and to conceal those responsible. [W-C018]
The Judiciary Committee adopted a second article alleging abuse of presidential powers and a third article alleging failure to comply with committee subpoenas. [W-C020]
On 9 August 1974, Richard Nixon resigned the office of President of the United States by letter to the Secretary of State. [W-C022]
On 8 September 1974, President Ford granted Richard Nixon a full, free, and absolute pardon for federal offenses he had committed or may have committed during his presidency. [W-C023]

Congress enacted the Presidential Recordings and Materials Preservation Act in 1974, placing Nixon presidential materials in federal custody and requiring priority processing of materials relating to Watergate and abuses of power. [W-C024]
The House authorized its Judiciary Committee on 6 February 1974 to investigate whether sufficient grounds existed to impeach President Nixon. [W-C028]

payload.mechanism: This is represented as a contemporary explanation and tested against later primary evidence and official findings.
payload.statement: The August 1972 public explanation that a White House inquiry found no White House personnel involved adequately described the matter.

payload.mechanism: The hypothesis separates Dean's allegation when made from the later tape, grand-jury evidence package, and Judiciary Committee majority findings.
payload.statement: Later primary evidence and official findings support that the Watergate matter included a course of conduct to impede investigation and conceal responsibility, beyond the original burglary.
The dispute over access to presidential recordings produced institutional and constitutional consequences involving Congress, the courts, the presidency, and preservation of presidential records.

The record must preserve competing views and procedural limits: committee findings were not unanimous, the full impeachment process did not reach judgment, and some recording questions remain unresolved.
